analogy.name: Opening a restaurant for the day
analogy.line: Booting is like opening a restaurant: the landlord unlocks the building, the manager picks the plan, staff arrive, then the host seats you.

linux.caption: A Linux boot is five handoffs in a row. If the box will not start, find the last handoff that worked and the next one is your suspect.
steps: The landlord unlocks the door. Firmware (UEFI) finds the boot disk and starts the bootloader. If it cannot find a disk, nothing else can begin.
The manager picks the day's plan. GRUB chooses a kernel, and you can pick an older one. That is your escape hatch after a bad update.
The kitchen crew arrives and the pantry opens. The kernel loads drivers and mounts the root filesystem. No root mount means no boot.
The manager hands out jobs. systemd is PID 1 and starts every service in dependency order. A failed unit here explains most half-booted boxes.
The host seats you. getty offers a login prompt and your shell starts. If you can type here, the other four handoffs worked.

analogy.name: A pre-flight checklist
analogy.line: A safe script is like a pilot's checklist: check the plane, rehearse, fly and log it, and raise the alarm the moment something is wrong.

scripting.caption: A production script checks its inputs, can dry-run, logs what it did and fails loudly. Silence is the bug.
steps: The walk-around before takeoff. You validate arguments, files and the target host first. A script that guesses can delete the wrong thing in prod.
The simulator run. A dry run prints what would change and changes nothing. Operators trust a script more when they can preview it.
The flight with a logbook. The script does the work and records what ran, what changed and what was skipped. That log is your audit trail.
The alarm. A non-zero exit code and a clear message say what failed. Silent failure lets a broken script run for weeks unnoticed.

analogy.name: A theme park wristband
analogy.line: Kerberos is like a park wristband: you prove who you are once at the gate, then show the band at each ride. The ride checks if you may enter.

windows.caption: Kerberos is the proof. The client shows a ticket, the server trusts the domain controller that signed it, and no password crosses the wire.
steps: You walk up to a ride. The client asks for a resource such as a share, a server or an app. Everything in a logon starts with a request like this.
You find the ticket booth. DNS tells the client which domain controller to use. When AD logons fail, broken DNS is a very common cause.
The booth checks your ID. The domain controller confirms who you are and issues the ticket. It is the authority every server in the domain trusts.
The wristband is the proof. The Kerberos ticket shows who you are without sending your password. This is why it is safer than sending credentials each time.
The ride checks the rules. The resource decides access from its own permissions. Being authenticated does not mean being authorised.

analogy.name: Sending a parcel by post
analogy.line: A network is like the post: you write the letter, a courier makes sure it arrives intact, the sorting office routes it, and the van drives it.

network.caption: Four layers, each with one job. When something breaks, name the layer first and the search space halves.
steps: The letter itself. The application layer carries what you care about, such as HTTP or DNS. Errors like 404 live here, not in the network.
The courier who checks delivery. TCP numbers the pieces, resends lost ones and keeps order. UDP skips that, which is why it is faster but less careful.
The sorting office. IP addresses and routing decide how a packet finds the far side. Ping and traceroute test this layer.
The delivery van and the road. Ethernet and Wi-Fi move frames to the next hop. An unplugged cable breaks every layer above it.

analogy.name: A restaurant host
analogy.line: A load balancer is like a host at the door: guests ask for one restaurant, and the host seats them at open tables and skips any closed section.

lb.caption: The load balancer's real job is not spreading load. It is noticing a dead backend before your users do.
steps: The guest arrives. The client uses one name and one address and never chooses a server. That makes adding or removing backends invisible to users.
The host at the door. The load balancer spreads requests and, more importantly, health-checks every backend. Tuning those checks is most of the real work.
The open tables. Only backends that pass the health check get traffic, and a failed one is removed quietly. This is how one server can die unnoticed.
The meal arrives. The client gets its answer without knowing which backend served it. That is also why you check LB logs to find which one did.

analogy.name: A recipe, frozen meal and served plate
analogy.line: A Dockerfile is the recipe, the image is the frozen meal made from it, and a container is that meal heated and served.

docker.caption: A Dockerfile is a recipe, an image is the frozen meal, a container is the meal served. Same image, same behaviour, anywhere.
steps: The recipe card. A Dockerfile lists the base image, files and commands in order. It is text you can version and review like any code.
Cooking step by step. Each instruction builds a cached layer, so a small change rebuilds only the end. Put rarely changing steps first for fast builds.
The frozen meal. The image is the finished, versioned result, identical on every machine. That is what you push to a registry and promote between environments.
The meal served. A container is an image running in isolation. The same image behaves the same on a laptop and in prod, which ends works-on-my-machine.

analogy.name: A hotel with a front desk
analogy.line: Kubernetes is like a hotel: the management office decides who works where, guests call the front desk, and staff are swapped without guests noticing.

k8s.caption: You talk to the Service, never to a pod directly. If a pod dies, the ReplicaSet starts another and the Service keeps pointing at the healthy set.
steps: The management office. The control plane (API server, scheduler, etcd) holds the desired state and decides what runs where. It does not serve your traffic itself.
The front desk number. A Service is a stable address that routes to matching pods. Because pod IPs change, callers must use the Service, never a pod.
The staff on shift. Pods come and go, and the ReplicaSet keeps three running. Replacing a dead pod automatically is the self-healing interviewers ask about.

analogy.name: A factory conveyor belt
analogy.line: A pipeline is like a conveyor belt: parts go in at one end, are inspected and packed once, then shipped with a way to recall them quickly.

cicd.caption: CI proves the change works. CD proves it works in production, by deploying in a way you can undo in seconds.
steps: A part lands on the belt. A commit to main starts the pipeline by itself. Automatic triggering means no step depends on someone remembering to run it.
The inspection station. Build and test run here, and a failure stops the belt before anything reaches users. Fast feedback keeps fixes cheap.
One sealed box. The artifact is built once and deployed to every environment. Rebuilding per environment lets differences creep in, which is drift.
The shipment with a recall. Blue-green or similar sends traffic to the new version while the old stays ready. Rollback becomes a switch, not a rebuild.

analogy.name: A hospital patient monitor
analogy.line: Monitoring is like a hospital monitor: sensors read vitals, a station gathers them, an alarm trips on danger, and the right nurse responds.

monitoring.caption: Monitoring is a pipeline: instrument, collect, alert, respond. An alert nobody acts on is just noise with a pager attached.
steps: The sensors on the patient. The app emits metrics and logs. If something is not measured, you cannot alert on it or prove it was healthy.
The nurses' station. Prometheus scrapes targets on a schedule and stores the numbers. Pull means the server controls its own load.
The alarm threshold. A rule fires when a symptom such as latency or errors crosses a line. Alert on what users feel, not on every internal blip.
The nurse on call. The page goes to the owner with a runbook link, so one person acts with context. Everyone else gets to sleep.

analogy.name: A shop with a counter and a vault
analogy.line: A 3-tier app is like a shop: customers meet the counter, staff on the floor do the work, and the stock sits in a vault only staff can reach.

cloud.caption: Three tiers, one rule: the client only ever talks to the load balancer, and the database only ever talks to the app.
steps: The customer at the street door. The client sees one public address and nothing behind it. Hiding the inside keeps the attack surface small.
The counter and the shop floor. The load balancer spreads traffic across identical app servers, so one can fail unnoticed. Identical servers are what make that safe.
The vault. A managed database that only the app can reach, never the client. Keeping the data tier private is a standard security answer.

analogy.name: Opening a new shop branch
analogy.line: Onboarding is like opening a shop branch: ask what it needs, size the premises, fit it out, connect utilities, open the doors, then hand over the keys.

onboarding.caption: Onboarding is a pipeline with a checklist at each gate. The failures are almost always the boring bits: DNS, TLS and who owns the app afterwards.
steps: The planning meeting. Intake means asking about ports, data, secrets and owners before you build. Missing answers here turn into delays at go-live.
Choosing the premises. You decide size and where it runs. This is the choice that is costly to undo, so it gets the most thought.
Fitting out the shop. You build a VM or containers, whichever suits how the app is operated. Both are valid, so choose on operations, not fashion.
Connecting water and power. DNS, the load balancer and TLS are the unglamorous bits that most often sink a go-live. Check them early.
Opening day and the handover. You cut over, watch it, then give support a runbook. A written handover beats a phone call every time.

analogy.name: A doctor's diagnosis
analogy.line: Troubleshooting is like a doctor's visit: see the symptom, narrow down the system, form one theory, try one treatment, then check the patient.

troubleshoot.caption: Troubleshooting is not guessing. Reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, fix one thing, verify. Skip a step and you fix the wrong thing twice.
steps: Seeing the symptom. You make the failure happen yourself. If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot show later that you fixed it.
Narrowing to one system. Find which phase is slow: DNS, connect, send, wait or receive. The phase points at the suspect.
One theory at a time. You form a single cause and a single test for it. Changing two things at once teaches you nothing.
One treatment. Make a small, reversible change and log it. If it makes things worse, you know exactly what to undo.
The follow-up check. Prove it works under the same conditions, then close it with a note for next time. A fix you never verified is only a hope.

analogy.name: A bookmark and a photocopy
analogy.line: A snapshot is like a bookmark in a book, a backup is like a photocopy kept in another building. Lose the book and the bookmark goes with it.

virt.caption: A snapshot is a bookmark that dies with the disk it points at. A backup is a copy somewhere else. Only one survives a dead host.
steps: The bookmark. A snapshot marks a point in time on the same storage. It is quick to take and revert, but long-lived ones slow the VM and share its fate.
The photocopy in another building. A backup lives elsewhere, so it survives the host, the array and the site. It is slower to restore, but it is the real protection.

analogy.name: A building with a guard at every door
analogy.line: Zero trust is like a building where every door has its own guard: showing a badge at the front gate does not open the server room.

security.caption: Zero trust means no layer vouches for another. Identity, device, network and data each prove themselves every time.
steps: The badge check. Identity asks who you are, with more than a password, such as MFA. It is the first control because stolen passwords are so common.
The health check at the door. The device must be managed, patched and healthy. A good user on a bad laptop is still a risk.
Locked doors between rooms. The network is segmented, so a breach in one corner cannot walk everywhere. This limits the blast radius.
The safe in the room. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, with keys you can rotate. If everything else fails, it is still unreadable.

analogy.name: A chess player's plan
analogy.line: Answering a scenario is like playing chess: read the board, choose a plan, make moves in order, and check the position before you finish.

scenarios.caption: Senior scenarios are not knowledge tests. They are structure tests: listen, pick a shape, answer in order, then check you landed it.
steps: Reading the board. Listen for what is really being asked, and restate it if unsure. Answering the wrong question loses marks however good the answer.
Choosing a plan. Pick a shape before you speak, such as STAR for stories or pros and cons for decisions. Structure signals seniority.
Making moves in order. Cover one point at a time in the order you promised. Wandering makes a correct answer sound unsure.
Checking the position. Ask if that answered it and close in one line. It leaves room for the follow-up and shows you are listening.
